author.name: Ruben J. Nazario, M.D., MBA
author.headline: Physician Executive | Clinical Informatics & Healthcare Technology Leader | Driving Clinical Strategy Across Payer–Provider Platforms | AI, Data, Value-Based Care

comments.text:
Ryan Howells, Nothing like a mandate to get things going!  A mandate would certainly give PIQI legs.

Having evaluated it against our framework at Availity, the one key gap I saw in the PIQI handbook is severity: PIQI uses pass/fail SAMs with a criticality boolean. That works for a scorecard, which is a good, digestible format that tells you your score, but it's harder to operationalize as a remediation framework that tells you what to fix, in what order, and why it matters clinically. For example, a missing onset date on an inactive problem is not the same failure as a missing SNOMED code on a condition driving HCC capture.

Our framework (375+ rules across C-CDA and HL7v2) grades every rule as Minor, Significant, or Critical, supports partial credit at the element level, and includes Patient Safety Indication flags, because some data quality failures pose clinical risk, not just interoperability friction.

Also: PIQI is scoped to single-message evaluation. Longitudinal quality is where most HEDIS and risk-adjustment gaps actually reside.

Solid foundation. Certification requirements should be explicit about what floor they're setting, and what they're leaving for the next layer.

author.name: dr. William Goossen FHL7
author.headline: Health informatician

comments.text:
it really depends on the goal of data use on the target side. If for aggregate purposes some data on source side would have been ignored anyway. Not “missed” but declared “irrelevant”. If for historic records, old data might be less relevant today. E.g. a blood pressure value of 1997 might not be of interest in 2026. For actual records, most data will be semantically mappable. And those who still “miss” could simply be re-entered in the current record using the actual semantics and codes.
This by the way has nothing to do with FHIR perse, but all with SnomedCT etc, clinical information modelling, and for the mapping, with the representation of these semantics in FHIR profiles.

author.name: Ryan Howells
author.headline: Health Care Policy | Strategy | Technology Leader | Kill the Clipboard!

comments.text:
The data quality scorecard needs to be open so there is a minimum degree of normalization across systems at the source before the data moves downstream. Of course our hope is PIQI will be used voluntarily and regs won’t be needed but the same scorecard needs to be used by everyone and the only way to do that is via an open standard and federal regs. The implications of not doing so means the cost of training the AI models to do effective and trustworthy CDS will be too expensive for most clinicians to bear.

The tools built on top of the open scorecard to determine how the data should be remediated, the severity of the data issues, and the specific use cases for how the data will be used will likely be proprietary based on unique needs. We are actively working with NCQA who said publicly they will be integrating PIQI into HEDIS reporting and the new iteration of PSV.

Our hope is your framework (and anyone else’s for that matter) uses PIQI as the common floor, not the ceiling.

comments.text:
Great write-up for the US, with very visible parallels to my European reality. Thanks Josh!

I know it is slightly off topic, but I would hope clinicians would take the lead in how data should be recorded at the source. This in itself impacts the clinical usefulness of the data when exchanged outside the original point of care.

Liesbeth Siderius presented on this topic during the recent IPS Summit in Brussels. For a patient summary to be able to contain and convey useful information, the underlying data needs to be recorded in such a way that it can be communicated and consumed intelligently.

Full report on the summit: https://international-patient-summary.net/ips-summit-in-brussels/

comments.text:
Josh Mandel, MD Categorization is definitely one source of the problem (USCDI_Clinical Notes being a great example). But there are also other causes, like EHR “template” workflows which results in data getting categorized too broadly (using LOINC as an example) and health data is too sensitive to eliminate this constraint IMO (EHI export was created for this right?).

Whether the issue is data access or data quality; specs, IGs and certification standards are only part of the equation. We need modern technology (agentic scribes, new data platforms, etc) to do the rest. Its still early, but I’m optimistic over the long term.

I’ve so many projects where the effort to map data and the quantity of data lost have both been wildly underestimated.

I want to believe that shared valuesets which are kept in sync between systems via a mechanism like subscriptions could solve part of this problem.

That said, I think your structural fix is more practical. Let the app get data and structure it themselves. However this approach is not without some obvious risks like getting data you’re not supposed to, or structuring it wrong and eliminating some important data that was relevant to patient care

author.name: Brian Pech

comments.text:
Yes, They Did
In September 2010, Kaiser Permanente donated its Convergent Medical Terminology (CMT) to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the International Health Terminology Standards Development Organisation (IHTSDO).
As part of this arrangement, the National Library of Medicine (NLM)—which acts as the U.S. member of the IHTSDO—distributes these terminology files and mappings to U.S. users.
What Was Included in the Donation?
Kaiser Permanente spent years developing CMT to act as a "translation engine" for electronic health records (EHRs). The donation provided healthcare organizations free access to:
Clinician-Friendly Terms: The display names used by doctors and nurses in Kaiser's own EHR systems.
Patient-Friendly Terms: Simplified medical terms that patients see in their personal health record (PHR) portals.
Standardized Mappings: Direct cross-maps linking these friendly terms to standardized national and international vocabularies, heavily featuring SNOMED CT, as well as mappings to ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM.
Tooling: Processes and tools used to create, manage, and control the quality of the medical terminology.
Why It Matters
The goal of this donation was to help other U.S.

comments.text: Ruben J. Nazario, M.D., MBA - PIQI does does not have severity, in part because we chose a model that aligns with digital quality measures - a simple numerator denominator.  In PIQI we assess what we need to use the data.  I something is a "nice to have" or 'low/minor' severity why bother scoring it - just measure it as informational.  I would also point out that some of what you are doing is outside of the mission scope for PIQI.  PIQI Framework was created to establish a open methodology to articulate and measure  minimal usability of data in a payload for a given use case.  Aggregation, be it categorical, longitudinal or geographical is trivial.  Once we have an objective, standards-based score with traceable causality, the stats nerds (me included) 🤓 can have their field day.  It has been great seeing members of your team testing PIQI at the connect-a-thons - asking questions and kicking the tires.  I am sure you and your team have done significant work in this space and we would love it if you would consider joining the #PIQIAlliance and helping us make PIQI even better.  Regardless, I appreciate your perspective and feedback.

comments.text: Josh Mandel, MD Yes, the problem exists as you point out. Words matter regarding the source of the problem and solution. For the problem you say:  “Every step that requires a provider to map internal codes to external standards is a step where data drops out.” For the solution you say “At each provider organization, someone maintains the mapping from internal codes”. I hold the vendors accountable for this problem, not the provider. I used to chair the general assembly at SNOMED International. I need more than 10 fingers to count how many times leaders from other countries asked my how does your country implement SNOMED. I said we don’t. We hold the vendors accountable for implementation.
